title: Abelian Categories
text:
Lemma (Four Lemma 1). For abelian groups \(A,B,C,D,A',B',C',D'\) and a commmutative diagram \[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[d, "\alpha", two heads] \arrow[r, "a"] & B \arrow[d, "\beta", hook] \arrow[r, "b"] & C \arrow[d, "\gamma"] \arrow[r, "c"] & D \arrow[d, "\delta", hook] \\
A' \arrow[r, "a'"]                              & B' \arrow[r, "b'"]                        & C' \arrow[r, "c'"]                   & D'                         
\end{tikzcd}
\] Where \(\beta, \delta\) are injective, \(\alpha\) surjective and the rows are exact, meaning \(f(x)=0 \iff \exists y, x=g(y)\) for any composable pair \(f,g\) in the row, then \(\gamma\) is injective.


Proof.

Suppose \(\gamma(x)=0\) then \(0=c'(\gamma(x))=\delta ( c(x))\) hense \(c(x)=0\) so by exactness there is some \(y\) so that \(x=b(y)\). This means \(0=\gamma ( b(y)) = b' (\beta(y))\) so by exactness there is some \(z\) so that \(a'(z)=\beta(y)\). As \(\alpha\) is surjective there is some \(w\) so that \(\alpha(w)=z\), here we have \(\beta (a(w))=a'(\alpha(w))=a'(z)=\beta(y)\) hense \(a(w)=y\) so by exactness \(0=b( a (w)) = b(y) = x\) hense \(\gamma(x)=0 \implies x=0\) so \(\gamma\) is injective

Now as it stands this is a pretty specific proof to abelian groups, well it also generalises to modules over a ring, or more generally some type of sets with structure such that \(\ker f = 0\) means \(f\) injective but if we try hard we can find different theorems of the same flavour for whom this proof doesn’t seem to work but yet still hold true
Lemma (Four Lemma 2). For abelian groups \(A,B,C,D,A',B',C',D'\) and a commmutative diagram \[
\begin{tikzcd}
A                             & B \arrow[l, "a"']                                  & C \arrow[l, "b"']                        & D \arrow[l, "c"']                                   \\
A' \arrow[u, "\alpha"', hook] & B' \arrow[u, "\beta"', two heads] \arrow[l, "a'"'] & C' \arrow[u, "\gamma"'] \arrow[l, "b'"'] & D' \arrow[u, "\delta"', two heads] \arrow[l, "c'"']
\end{tikzcd}
\] Where \(\beta, \delta\) are surjective, \(\alpha\) injective and the rows are exact, meaning \(f(x)=0 \iff \exists y, x=g(y)\) for any composable pair \(f,g\) in the row, then \(\gamma\) is surjective.


Proof.

Ok so I’m lying a little bit here you can prove this one the same way once you use Pontryagin duality to show \(\mathbf{Ab}^{op} \cong \mathbf{CTop}_{Ab}\) and then the original proof works there

Lemma (Four Lemma 1). Let \((X,\mathcal{T})\) be a topological space, a sheaf is a function \(\mathcal{F}\colon\mathcal{T} \to \mathbf{Ab}\) such that any subset inclusion \(U \subset V\) induces a group homomorphism \(\mathcal{F}(V) \to \mathcal{F}(U)\) which is coherent with taking further subsets, and if you have elements of \(\mathcal{F}(U),\mathcal{F}(V)\) that agree on these “restriction maps” to the intersection we get a unique element of \(\mathcal{F}(U \cup V)\). Maps between sheaves are then a family of maps \(\mathcal{F}(U) \to \mathcal{G}(U)\) that are group homs and agree with restriction. For such sheaves \(A,B,C,D,A',B',C',D'\) and a commmutative diagram \[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[d, "\alpha", two heads] \arrow[r, "a"] & B \arrow[d, "\beta", hook] \arrow[r, "b"] & C \arrow[d, "\gamma"] \arrow[r, "c"] & D \arrow[d, "\delta", hook] \\
A' \arrow[r, "a'"]                              & B' \arrow[r, "b'"]                        & C' \arrow[r, "c'"]                   & D'                         
\end{tikzcd}
\] Where \(\beta, \delta\) are injective on each \(\mathcal{F}(U)\), \(\alpha\) surjective on each \(\mathcal{F}_x =\lim_{x \in U}\mathcal{F}(U)\) for \(x \in X\) and the rows are exact, meaning, at every \(\mathcal{F}_x\), \(f(x)=0 \iff \exists y, x=g(y)\) for any composable pair \(f,g\) in the row, then \(\gamma\) is injective.


Proof.

This one does require some theory, although I ask that for now you accept that this structure on the category of sheaves gives the correct notions of injective/surjective/exact

And of course this one has the opposite as well, in order to prove such a thing it would be mighty convenient to have a general setup that makes rigourous the calculations done in the first proof. For this we introduce the notion of an abelian category and take two approaches, one requires some subtlelty in application to use the notion of generalised elements, and the other is wonderful in how lazy one can be when using it. title: Universal algebra
text:
Lawvere theories and their models
Definition. A Lawvere theory is a small category \(\mathcal T\) with finite coproducts and a specified object \(T \in \mathcal T\), such that the objects of \(\mathcal T\) precisely form the set \(\{0,\, T,\, T + T,\, T + T + T,\, \dots, \sum_{i < n} T, \dots\}\). For a category \(\mathcal{C}\) with finite products, a \(\mathcal{C}\)-model of a Lawvere theory \(\mathcal T\) is a functor \(M \colon \mathcal T^\mathrm{op}\to \mathcal{C}\) which preserves finite products. We denote by \(\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathcal T}(\mathcal{C})\) the full subcategory of the functor category \([\mathcal T, \mathcal{C}]\) consisting of all the \(\mathcal{C}\)-models of \(\mathcal T\). We may drop the mention of \(\mathcal{C}\) when it is clear from context; we will often take \(\mathcal{C}= \mathbf{Set}\).
Example. For each natural number \(n \in \mathbb N\), let \([n] \in \mathbf{Set}\) denote the a set of cardinality \(n\). Consider the free–forgetful adjunction \(\mathbf{Set} \substack{\xrightarrow{F} \\ \perp \\ \xleftarrow[U]{}} \mathbf{Grp}\), and let \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{Grp}}\) denote the full subcategory of \(\mathbf{Grp}\) consisting of each \(F[n]\) for all \(n \in \mathbb N\). Then we have an equivalence of categories \(\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathcal T_{\mathrm{Grp}}}(\mathbf{Set}) \simeq \mathbf{Grp}\).


Details.

First, we observe that \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{Grp}}\) is indeed a Lawvere theory. For each \(n \in \mathbb N\), we have \([n] \cong \sum_{i < n} [1]\) in \(\mathbf{Set}\). So \(F[n] \cong \sum_{i < n} F[1]\) in \(\mathbf{Grp}\), since \(F\) preserves coproducts. Thus we get \(F[n] = \sum_{i < n} F[1]\) in \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{Grp}}\).
Next, given a \(\mathbf{Set}\)-model \(M \colon \mathcal T_\mathrm{Grp}^\mathrm{op}\to \mathbf{Set}\), let \(HM\) be the group with:
1. underlying set \(MF[1]\);
2. group multiplication \(M\alpha \colon (MF[1]) \times (MF[1]) \to MF[1]\), where \(\alpha \colon F[1] \to F[1] + F[1] = F[2]\) is the map in \(\mathcal T_\mathrm{Grp}\) sending the generator of \(F[1]\) to the multiplication of the two generators in \(F[2]\);
3. identity element \((Me)(*) \in MF[1]\), where \(*\) is the unique element in \((MF[1])^0\), and \(e \colon F[1] \to F[0]\) is the unique map in \(\mathcal T_\mathrm{Grp}\) from \(F[1]\) to \(F[0]\).



Check that \(HM\) is a group.


We extend \(H\) to a functor \(H \colon \mathbf{Mod}_{\mathcal T_{\mathrm{Grp}}}(\mathbf{Set}) \to \mathbf{Grp}\) as follows: given another \(M' \in \mathbf{Mod}_{\mathcal T_\mathrm{Grp}}(\mathbf{Set})\) and a morphism \(\mu \colon M \to M'\) in \(\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathcal T_\mathrm{Grp}}(\mathbf{Set})\), let \(H\mu\) be the function \(\mu_{F[1]} \colon MF[1] \to M'F[1]\).


Check that \(H\mu\) is a group homomorphism.

The commutativity of the diagram
